newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters back at bargaining table Thursday.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters back at bargaining table Thursday.

text.p: The Teamsters and United Parcel Service will return to the bargaining table on Thursday in a third attempt to end the 11-day-old strike, one of the largest in the past quarter century.
The two sides were to meet at 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) with federal mediator John Calhoun Wells, who has moderated the past two unsuccessful rounds of talks.

Labor Secretary Alexis Herman is urging both sides to keep talking until they reach agreement on a new contract for some 185,000 union workers who are demanding the company shift more of its work into full-time jobs.
But Teamsters President Ron Carey doubted that the meeting would end the strike, which has already cost UPS hundreds of millions of dollars.

"While there is no reason for optimism at this point, we will be there, ready to negotiate a reasonable agreement that provides the good jobs that American families need," Carey said in a statement late on Wednesday.
Herman said that "the key now is for both parties to find a new way to look at the issues and find a solution at the table," and she urged them "to stay at the table until they reach a settlement."
Talks broke off on Saturday, when UPS Chairman James Kelly left the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, calling the Teamster position "unrealistic."
Kelly issued a statement late on Wednesday saying the company remained "open and willing to examine all avenues that will help our people get back to work."
The strike began Aug. 4 after the two sides failed to reach common ground on issues including subcontracting, the number of part-time workers, and a new pension plan.

Herman called both sides into her office this week and they met on Monday. But the two sides hardened their positions on Tuesday, when the AFL-CIO offered millions of dollars to help the Teamsters pay strike benefits to people on picket lines and UPS warned it will cut 15,000 jobs due to lost business.
President Bill Clinton has refused to intervene in the strike, with administration officials repeatedly saying the situation did not comprise a national emergency.
But the strike is causing tough consequences around the country. Several smaller firms have announced layoffs because they cannot get their goods to consumers.
Russ Berrie and Co. Inc., a New Jersey-based maker of plush dolls and gift items, and National TechTeam Inc., which provides technical services to UPS customers, each said they cut about 100 workers.
The Independent Pilots Association of UPS pilots -- which has refused to cross Teamster picket lines to fly 500 UPS planes -- issued a warning to pilots whose airlines were carrying UPS packages.
"Effective on Friday, Aug. 15 ... all flights carrying struck UPS goods will be considered strike-breaking activity," the union said. It scheduled a news conference for Thursday.
